claim: Sensory neurons with cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia (DRG) represent a useful model to study axon regeneration.
source: Sensory neurons with cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia (DRG) represent a useful model to study axon regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field of neuroscience research.

claim: Regeneration and functional recovery occurs after peripheral nerve injury.
source: Whereas regeneration and functional recovery occurs after peripheral nerve injury, spinal cord injury or dorsal root injury is not followed by regenerative outcomes.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the field, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Spinal cord injury is not followed by regenerative outcomes.
source: Whereas regeneration and functional recovery occurs after peripheral nerve injury, spinal cord injury or dorsal root injury is not followed by regenerative outcomes.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the field, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Dorsal root injury is not followed by regenerative outcomes.
source: Whereas regeneration and functional recovery occurs after peripheral nerve injury, spinal cord injury or dorsal root injury is not followed by regenerative outcomes.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the field, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: All injuries increased the proportion of a cell type that shares features of both immune cells and glial cells.
source: All injuries increased the proportion of a cell type that shares features of both immune cells and glial cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's single-cell transcriptional profiling data.

claim: A distinct subset of satellite glial cells (SGC) appeared specifically in response to peripheral nerve injury.
source: A distinct subset of satellite glial cells (SGC) appeared specifically in response to peripheral nerve injury.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's single-cell transcriptional profiling data.

claim: Activation of the PPARα signaling pathway in SGC promotes axon regeneration after peripheral nerve injury.
source: Activation of the PPARα signaling pathway in SGC, which promotes axon regeneration after peripheral nerve injury, failed to occur after central axon injuries.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors and supported by citations.

claim: Activation of the PPARα signaling pathway in SGC failed to occur after central axon injuries.
source: Activation of the PPARα signaling pathway in SGC, which promotes axon regeneration after peripheral nerve injury, failed to occur after central axon injuries.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's single-cell transcriptional profiling data.

claim: Treatment with the FDA-approved PPARα agonist fenofibrate increased axon regeneration after dorsal root injury.
source: Treatment with the FDA-approved PPARα agonist fenofibrate increased axon regeneration after dorsal root injury.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Sensory neurons send a single axon which bifurcates within the ganglion; one axon proceeds centrally along the dorsal root into the spinal cord and the other proceeds along peripheral nerves.
source: Sensory neurons send a single axon which bifurcates within the ganglion; one axon proceeds centrally along the dorsal root into the spinal cord and the other proceeds along peripheral nerves.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about sensory neurons.

claim: Central injury fails to elicit a pro-regenerative response in sensory neurons.
source: This results in part from a failure of central injury to elicit a pro-regenerative response in sensory neurons (Attwell et al., 2018; Fagoe et al., 2014; Mahar and Cavalli, 2018; Tran et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Dorsal root disruption can occur in brachial plexus injuries, leading to paralysis of the affected arm.
source: Dorsal root disruption can occur in brachial plexus injuries, leading to paralysis of the affected arm (Smith et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Regeneration following dorsal root crush can occur along the growth-supportive environment of Schwann cells, but stops as the axons reach the transition between the peripheral nervous system and the central nervous system, termed the dorsal root entry zone.
source: Regeneration following dorsal root crush can occur along the growth-supportive environment of Schwann cells, but stops as the axons reach the transition between the peripheral nervous system and the central nervous system, termed the dorsal root entry zone, where a variety of inhibitory factors block further growth (Smith et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Dorsal root axonal growth occurs only at half the rate of peripheral axons.
source: However dorsal root axonal growth occurs only at half the rate of peripheral axons (Oblinger and Lasek, 1984; Wujek and Lasek, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The histological difference between dorsal roots and peripheral nerve is not sufficient to alter the rate of axonal regeneration.
source: The histological difference between dorsal roots and peripheral nerve is not sufficient to alter the rate of axonal regeneration (Wujek and Lasek, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The availability of trophic factors and other target derived influences via the peripheral axon were suggested to prevent the upregulation of pro-regenerative genes such as Jun.
source: Rather, the availability of trophic factors and other target derived influences via the peripheral axon were suggested to prevent the upregulation of pro-regenerative genes such as Jun (Broude et al., 1997) or Gap43 (Schreyer and Skene, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Dorsal root injury causes up-regulation of the pro-regenerative gene Atf3, but only in large diameter neurons.
source: Interestingly, dorsal root injury causes up-regulation of the pro-regenerative gene Atf3 (Huang et al., 2006), but only in large diameter neurons, whereas Atf3 and Jun are upregulated in a majority of neurons after peripheral nerve injury (Chandran et al., 2016; Renthal et al., 2020; Seijffers et al., 2007; Tsujino et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Atf3 and Jun are upregulated in a majority of neurons after peripheral nerve injury.
source: Interestingly, dorsal root injury causes up-regulation of the pro-regenerative gene Atf3 (Huang et al., 2006), but only in large diameter neurons, whereas Atf3 and Jun are upregulated in a majority of neurons after peripheral nerve injury (Chandran et al., 2016; Renthal et al., 2020; Seijffers et al., 2007; Tsujino et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Spinal cord injury leads to activation of Atf3 in large diameter neurons, but this is not sufficient to promote regenerative growth.
source: Spinal cord injury also leads to activation of Atf3 in large diameter neurons, but this is not sufficient to promote regenerative growth (Ewan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Regeneration of axons in peripheral nerves is not cell autonomous.
source: Regeneration of axons in peripheral nerves is not cell autonomous.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: At the site of injury in the nerve, Schwann cells and macrophages contribute to promote axon regeneration.
source: At the site of injury in the nerve, Schwann cells (Jessen and Mirsky, 2016) and macrophages (Zigmond and Echevarria, 2019) contribute to promote axon regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Macrophages are involved in eliciting a pro-regenerative response after peripheral but not central injury.
source: In the DRG, macrophages are involved in eliciting a pro-regenerative response after peripheral but not central injury (Kwon et al., 2013; Niemi et al., 2016; Niemi et al., 2013; Zigmond and Echevarria, 2019), with anti-inflammatory macrophages believed to be more involved in the regenerative process than pro-inflammatory macrophages (Zigmond and Echevarria, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Anti-inflammatory macrophages are believed to be more involved in the regenerative process than pro-inflammatory macrophages.
source: In the DRG, macrophages are involved in eliciting a pro-regenerative response after peripheral but not central injury (Kwon et al., 2013; Niemi et al., 2016; Niemi et al., 2013; Zigmond and Echevarria, 2019), with anti-inflammatory macrophages believed to be more involved in the regenerative process than pro-inflammatory macrophages (Zigmond and Echevarria, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Satellite glial cells (SGC), which completely surround sensory neuron soma, contribute to promote axon regeneration.
source: We recently revealed that satellite glial cells (SGC), which completely surround sensory neuron soma, also contribute to promote axon regeneration (Avraham et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous research.

claim: PPARα signaling downstream of fatty acid synthase (FASN) in SGC promote axon regeneration in peripheral nerves, in part via regulating the expression of pro-regenerative genes in neurons, such as Atf3.
source: PPARα signaling downstream of fatty acid synthase (FASN) in SGC promote axon regeneration in peripheral nerves, in part via regulating the expression of pro-regenerative genes in neurons, such as Atf3 (Avraham et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous research.

claim: Sciatic nerve crush injures approximately half the axons projecting into the peripheral nerves.
source: Sciatic nerve crush injures approximately half the axons projecting into the peripheral nerves (Laedermann et al., 2014; Rigaud et al., 2008) and dorsal root crush injures all axons projecting into the dorsal root.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Dorsal root crush injures all axons projecting into the dorsal root.
source: Sciatic nerve crush injures approximately half the axons projecting into the peripheral nerves (Laedermann et al., 2014; Rigaud et al., 2008) and dorsal root crush injures all axons projecting into the dorsal root.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the injury model used in the study.

claim: Dorsal column lesion of the spinal cord damages the ascending axon branches of most large diameter neurons and leaves the descending axon branches in the spinal cord intact.
source: Dorsal column lesion of the spinal cord damages the ascending axon branches of most large diameter neurons and leaves the descending axon branches in the spinal cord intact (Attwell et al., 2018; Niu et al., 2013; Zheng et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Gene expression changes occurred in endothelial cells, pericytes, Schwann cells, macrophages and SGC after peripheral nerve injury.
source: We found that gene expression changes occurred in endothelial cells, pericytes, Schwann cells, macrophages and SGC after peripheral nerve injury, but also occurred after dorsal root crush and spinal cord injury.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's single-cell transcriptional profiling data.

claim: Gene expression changes occurred in endothelial cells, pericytes, Schwann cells, macrophages and SGC after dorsal root crush and spinal cord injury.
source: We found that gene expression changes occurred in endothelial cells, pericytes, Schwann cells, macrophages and SGC after peripheral nerve injury, but also occurred after dorsal root crush and spinal cord injury.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's single-cell transcriptional profiling data.

claim: Each cell type responded differently to each injury.
source: However, each cell type responded differently to each injury.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's single-cell transcriptional profiling data.

claim: SGC fail to activate the PPARα signaling pathway in response to dorsal root crush.
source: We show that SGC fail to activate the PPARα signaling pathway in response to dorsal root crush and downregulate this pathway in response to SCI.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's single-cell transcriptional profiling data.

claim: SGC downregulate the PPARα signaling pathway in response to SCI.
source: We show that SGC fail to activate the PPARα signaling pathway in response to dorsal root crush and downregulate this pathway in response to SCI.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's single-cell transcriptional profiling data.

claim: GFP-positive neurons represented only ~12.5% of all cells in dissociated DRG cells from Actl6bCre (Baf53bCre): Sun1GFP mice.
source: FACS sorting analysis of dissociated DRG cells from Actl6bCre (Baf53bCre): Sun1GFP in which GFP is expressed in the neuronal nuclei (Mo et al., 2015; Zhan et al., 2015) showed that GFP-positive neurons represented only ~12.5% of all cells (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from FACS sorting analysis presented in the study, with supporting figure reference.

claim: The number of total sequenced cells from all conditions was 25,154 from two biological replicates for naive, SCI and DRC conditions, and one biological replicate for SNC.
source: The number of total sequenced cells from all conditions was 25,154 from two biological replicates for naive, SCI and DRC conditions, and one biological replicate for SNC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), with an average of 45,000 reads per cell, 1500 genes per cell and a total of 17,879 genes detected (see filtering criteria in the methods).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data collected in the study.

claim: An unbiased (Graph-based) clustering identified 19 distinct cell clusters in the control and injured samples.
source: An unbiased (Graph-based) clustering, using Partek flow analysis package, identified 19 distinct cell clusters in the control and injured samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational analysis of the scRNAseq data.

claim: SGC and macrophages clusters contained the largest number of cells.
source: A t-SNE (t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding) plot of all 25,154 cells combined from naive and injury conditions revealed that SGC and macrophages clusters contained the largest number of cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational analysis of the scRNAseq data, with supporting figure reference.

claim: There was a reduction in the percentage of SGC after peripheral and central injuries.
source: Comparison of population distribution between the different injury conditions revealed a reduction in the percentage of SGC after peripheral and central injuries, with an increase in the number of macrophages compared to naive condition (Figure 1G and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational analysis of the scRNAseq data, with supporting figure reference.

claim: There was an increase in the number of macrophages after peripheral and central injuries compared to naive condition.
source: Comparison of population distribution between the different injury conditions revealed a reduction in the percentage of SGC after peripheral and central injuries, with an increase in the number of macrophages compared to naive condition (Figure 1G and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational analysis of the scRNAseq data, with supporting figure reference.

claim: The magnitude of gene expression changes was the largest after SNC, but also occurred after DRC and SCI.
source: Heat map of differential gene expression in the indicated cell types revealed that the magnitude of gene expression changes was the largest after SNC, but also occurred after DRC and SCI (Figure 1I and Figure 1—source data 1), as previously suggested (Palmisano et al., 2019; Stam et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational analysis of the scRNAseq data, with supporting figure reference and citations.

claim: The cell-cell interaction network changed significantly after SNC compared to naïve.
source: This analysis revealed that the cell-cell interaction network changed significantly after SNC compared to naïve, and that these changes are distinct from those elicit by DRC.
evidence: This is a finding from the cell-cell interaction analysis using CellPhoneDB.

claim: The changes in cell-cell interaction network after SNC are distinct from those elicited by DRC.
source: This analysis revealed that the cell-cell interaction network changed significantly after SNC compared to naïve, and that these changes are distinct from those elicit by DRC.
evidence: This is a finding from the cell-cell interaction analysis using CellPhoneDB.

claim: SCI had limited influence on the cellular network interaction compared to naive.
source: SCI had limited influence on the cellular network interaction compared to naive (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from the cell-cell interaction analysis using CellPhoneDB, with supporting figure reference.

claim: Blood-tissue barriers play an essential role in the maintenance and homeostasis of the tissue environment.
source: Blood-tissue barriers play an essential role in the maintenance and homeostasis of the tissue environment.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Integrity of the peripheral nervous system is maintained by the blood-nerve-barrier (BNB), which shares many structural features with the blood brain barrier.
source: Integrity of the peripheral nervous system is maintained by the blood-nerve-barrier (BNB), which shares many structural features with the blood brain barrier (Richner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: An essential component of the BNB cellular architecture is tight junctions (TJ) in the endoneurial vascular endothelium or the perineurium that surrounds the nerve fascicle.
source: An essential component of the BNB cellular architecture is tight junctions (TJ) in the endoneurial vascular endothelium or the perineurium that surrounds the nerve fascicle.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the blood-nerve barrier.

claim: Endothelial cells comprise the inner lining of vessels, while pericytes encompass blood microvessels such as blood capillaries.
source: Endothelial cells comprise the inner lining of vessels, while pericytes encompass blood microvessels such as blood capillaries (Sims, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Sensory ganglia are highly vascularized.
source: Sensory ganglia are highly vascularized (Figure 2A; Jimenez-Andrade et al., 2008), with blood vessels in sensory ganglia being more permeable than their counterpart in the brain (Kiernan, 1996; Reinhold and Rittner, 2017) or the nerve (Hirakawa et al., 2004; Jimenez-Andrade et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and a figure reference.

claim: Blood vessels in sensory ganglia are more permeable than their counterpart in the brain or the nerve.
source: Sensory ganglia are highly vascularized (Figure 2A; Jimenez-Andrade et al., 2008), with blood vessels in sensory ganglia being more permeable than their counterpart in the brain (Kiernan, 1996; Reinhold and Rittner, 2017) or the nerve (Hirakawa et al., 2004; Jimenez-Andrade et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Pericytes do not fully cover the blood vessel in peripheral nerve.
source: Unlike in the brain, pericytes do not fully cover the blood vessel in peripheral nerve (Stierli et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The presence of blood vessel not fully covered by pericytes was observed in the DRG.
source: We observed a similar situation in the DRG, with the presence of blood vessel not fully covered by pericytes (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the TEM imaging data presented in the study, with supporting figure reference.

claim: t-SNE plots of endothelial cells and pericytes demonstrated different clustering of cells after SNC or DRC, while similar clustering in naïve and after SCI were observed.
source: t-SNE plots of endothelial cells and pericytes demonstrated different clustering of cells after SNC or DRC, while similar clustering in naïve and after SCI were observed (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational analysis of the scRNAseq data, with supporting figure reference.

claim: Increased BNB permeability in the nerve is linked to changes in the expression of TJ genes, in particular a reduced expression of ZO-1 (Tjp1) in endoneurial cells.
source: Increased BNB permeability in the nerve is linked to changes in the expression of TJ genes, in particular a reduced expression of ZO-1 (Tjp1) in endoneurial cells (Richner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The response of barrier components was affected by SNC differently than DRC, with numerous junction genes being differentially expressed following SNC and DRC compared to naive and SCI condition.
source: Heat map of TJ and AJ genes indicated that the response of barrier components was affected by SNC differently than DRC, with numerous junction genes being differentially expressed following SNC and DRC compared to naive and SCI condition (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational analysis of the scRNAseq data, with supporting figure reference.

claim: Changes in Tjp1 and Tjp2 expression suggest that the BNB may be more permeable after SNC and DRC compared to naive and SCI.
source: Changes in Tjp1 and Tjp2 expression suggest that the BNB may be more permeable after SNC and DRC compared to naive and SCI.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gene expression data.

claim: The enrichment of the cell cycle pathway after SNC and DRC suggests that endothelial cell division may regulate blood vessel angiogenesis.
source: The enrichment of the cell cycle pathway after SNC and DRC suggests that endothelial cell division may regulate blood vessel angiogenesis (Zeng et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pathway analysis data, supported by a citation.

claim: After nerve injury, dedifferentiation of Schwann cells into repair Schwann cells at the site of injury as well as resident macrophages in the nerve elicits breakdown of the BNB.
source: After nerve injury, dedifferentiation of Schwann cells into repair Schwann cells at the site of injury as well as resident macrophages in the nerve elicits breakdown of the BNB (Mellick and Cavanagh, 1968; Napoli et al., 2012; Richner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Schwann cells in the DRG undergo transcriptional changes that are distinct after peripheral and central injuries.
source: Although Schwann cells in the DRG are far away from the injury site in axons, we found that they undergo transcriptional changes that are distinct after peripheral and central injuries.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational analysis of the scRNAseq data.

claim: t-SNE plots demonstrated different clustering of Schwann cells in SNC and DRC conditions, with similar clustering in naïve and SCI.
source: t-SNE plots demonstrated different clustering of Schwann cells in SNC and DRC conditions, with similar clustering in naïve and SCI (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational analysis of the scRNAseq data, with supporting figure reference.

claim: Ngf, which is known to promote myelination by Schwann cells in peripheral nerves, is downregulated after all injuries.
source: Notably, Ngf, which is known to promote myelination by Schwann cells in peripheral nerves (Chan et al., 2004) is downregulated after all injuries.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq data, supported by a citation about NGF function.

claim: VEGF is known to increase BNB permeability.
source: VEGF is known to increase BNB permeability (Lim et al., 2014) and Vegfb is differentially regulated after peripheral and central injuries (Figure 2J), suggesting that Schwann cells may influence BNB permeability in the DRG.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Vegfb is differentially regulated after peripheral and central injuries.
source: VEGF is known to increase BNB permeability (Lim et al., 2014) and Vegfb is differentially regulated after peripheral and central injuries (Figure 2J), suggesting that Schwann cells may influence BNB permeability in the DRG.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq data, with supporting figure reference.

claim: Schwann cells may influence BNB permeability in the DRG.
source: VEGF is known to increase BNB permeability (Lim et al., 2014) and Vegfb is differentially regulated after peripheral and central injuries (Figure 2J), suggesting that Schwann cells may influence BNB permeability in the DRG.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gene expression data and known functions of VEGF.

claim: Shh is strongly upregulated after DRC.
source: Shh is strongly upregulated after DRC.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq data.

claim: Shh signaling in Schwann cells in the DRG after SNC and DRC may have neuroprotective functions.
source: Shh signaling in Schwann cells in the DRG after SNC and DRC may have neuroprotective functions (Hashimoto et al., 2008) and may facilitate axon regeneration (Martinez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation based on citations to previous research.

claim: Shh signaling may facilitate axon regeneration.
source: Shh signaling in Schwann cells in the DRG after SNC and DRC may have neuroprotective functions (Hashimoto et al., 2008) and may facilitate axon regeneration (Martinez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation based on citations to previous research.

claim: The hedgehog signaling pathway and axon guidance is upregulated specifically after DRC.
source: KEGG analysis also revealed that the hedgehog signaling pathway and axon guidance is upregulated specifically after DRC (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is a finding from the KEGG pathway analysis of the scRNAseq data, with supporting figure reference.

claim: The hippo signaling pathway is downregulated specifically after SCI and DRC.
source: The hippo signaling pathway, which plays multiple cellular functions, such as proliferation, apoptosis, regeneration, and organ size control (Yu and Guan, 2013; Zhao et al., 2011), is downregulated specifically after SCI and DRC.
evidence: This is a finding from the KEGG pathway analysis of the scRNAseq data, with citations about the pathway's functions.

claim: Key transcription factors in the Hippo pathway, Yap and Bmp5 were downregulated after DRC and SCI, and upregulated after SNC.
source: Key transcription factors in the Hippo pathway, Yap and Bmp5 were downregulated after DRC and SCI, and upregulated after SNC (FDR ≤ 0.05, FC ≥2) (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq data.

claim: Schwann cell in the DRG respond differently to peripheral and central injuries, with central injury potentially limiting their plasticity.
source: These results suggest that Schwann cell in the DRG respond differently to peripheral and central injuries, with central injury potentially limiting their plasticity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gene expression and pathway analysis data.

claim: After nerve injury, breakdown of the BNB allows the influx of inflammatory cells at the site of injury in the nerve to promote repair.
source: After nerve injury, breakdown of the BNB allows the influx of inflammatory cells at the site of injury in the nerve to promote repair (Mellick and Cavanagh, 1968; Napoli et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Macrophages regulate axon regeneration and pain responses acting at the level of the ganglia.
source: In addition to their role at the site of injury in the nerve, macrophages regulate axon regeneration and pain responses acting at the level of the ganglia (Kwon et al., 2013; Niemi et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Both resident and infiltrating macrophages were found in the DRG.
source: Both resident and infiltrating macrophages were found in the DRG (Zigmond and Echevarria, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Most DRG macrophages express the snMac1 genes (Cbrr2, Mgl2).
source: This analysis revealed that most DRG macrophages express the snMac1 genes (Cbrr2, Mgl2) (Figure 3A, light blue), whereas few DRG macrophages express the snMac2 genes (Retnnla, Clecl10a, Folr2) (Figure 3A, blue).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq data analysis, with supporting figure reference.

claim: Few DRG macrophages express the snMac2 genes (Retnnla, Clecl10a, Folr2).
source: This analysis revealed that most DRG macrophages express the snMac1 genes (Cbrr2, Mgl2) (Figure 3A, light blue), whereas few DRG macrophages express the snMac2 genes (Retnnla, Clecl10a, Folr2) (Figure 3A, blue).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq data analysis, with supporting figure reference.

claim: DRG macrophages express CNS associated microglia genes such as Tmem119, P2ry12, and Trem2.
source: The DRG macrophages, similarly to nerve macrophages (Wang et al., 2020; Ydens et al., 2020), also express CNS associated microglia genes such as Tmem119, P2ry12, and Trem2 (Figure 3A, pink) and common microglia/macrophages markers Ccl12,Gpr34, Gpr183, Hexb, Mef2c, St3gal6, and Tagap (Figure 3A, green).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq data analysis, with supporting figure reference and citations.

claim: The common macrophages markers Cd68, Emr1 and Aif1 were expressed in >80% of cells in the macrophage cluster.
source: The common macrophages markers Cd68, Emr1 and Aif1 were expressed in >80% of cells in the macrophage cluster (Figure 3A, orange and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq data analysis, with supporting figure reference.

claim: DRG macrophages share similar properties to snMac1 residing in the nerve endoneurium and with CNS microglia.
source: These results suggest that DRG macrophages share similar properties to snMac1 residing in the nerve endoneurium and with CNS microglia.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gene expression data.

claim: The number of macrophages increased after SNC compared to naïve and also increased to a lesser extent after DRC and SCI.
source: The number of macrophages increased after SNC compared to naïve and also increased to a lesser extent after DRC and SCI (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq data analysis, with supporting figure reference.

claim: Macrophages displayed a similar gene expression profile in naive and SCI condition, but SNC and DRC elicited large changes in genes expression.
source: Macrophages displayed a similar gene expression profile in naive and SCI condition, but SNC and DRC elicited large changes in genes expression (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq data analysis, with supporting figure reference.

claim: KEGG pathway analysis revealed upregulation of cell cycle and DNA replication after SNC.
source: KEGG pathway analysis of DE genes (FDR ≤ 0.05, FC ≥2) (Figure 3—source data 1) revealed upregulation of cell cycle and DNA replication after SNC, while DRC and SCI macrophages mainly showed upregulation of metabolic pathways such as steroid biosynthesis and glycolysis/gluconeogenesis pathways (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the KEGG pathway analysis of the scRNAseq data, with supporting figure reference.

claim: DRC and SCI macrophages mainly showed upregulation of metabolic pathways such as steroid biosynthesis and glycolysis/gluconeogenesis pathways.
source: KEGG pathway analysis of DE genes (FDR ≤ 0.05, FC ≥2) (Figure 3—source data 1) revealed upregulation of cell cycle and DNA replication after SNC, while DRC and SCI macrophages mainly showed upregulation of metabolic pathways such as steroid biosynthesis and glycolysis/gluconeogenesis pathways (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the KEGG pathway analysis of the scRNAseq data, with supporting figure reference.

claim: Macrophages from all injury conditions down regulated genes related to antigen processing and presentation as well as genes involved in phagosome activity.
source: Interestingly, macrophages from all injury conditions down regulated genes related to antigen processing and presentation as well as genes involved in phagosome activity (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the KEGG pathway analysis of the scRNAseq data, with supporting figure reference.

claim: The down regulation of genes involved in antigen processing and presentation associated with class II major histocompatibility complex (MHC II) Cd74, H2-Aa and Ctss was validated in qPCR experiments.
source: We further validated the down regulation of genes involved in antigen processing and presentation associated with class II major histocompatibility complex (MHC II) Cd74, H2-Aa and Ctss in qPCR experiments (Figure 3D and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the qPCR validation experiments, with supporting figure reference.

claim: Macrophages responses to injury in the DRG are complex and may not easily follow the classical pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory polarization scheme.
source: Heat map of cytokines and other macrophages polarization markers suggest that macrophages responses to injury in the DRG are complex and may not easily follow the classical pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory polarization scheme (Figure 3E and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gene expression data, with supporting figure reference.

claim: Expression of the anti-inflammatory marker gene Arg1 was only detected after DRC.
source: Furthermore, expression of the anti-inflammatory marker gene Arg1 was only detected after DRC and the pro-inflammatory marker Nos2 was not detected in any conditions (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq data analysis, with supporting figure reference.

claim: The pro-inflammatory marker Nos2 was not detected in any conditions.
source: Furthermore, expression of the anti-inflammatory marker gene Arg1 was only detected after DRC and the pro-inflammatory marker Nos2 was not detected in any conditions (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq data analysis, with supporting figure reference.

claim: Among the significant down regulated genes after SNC, the cytokines Ccl2, Il1b and Tnf were found.
source: Among the significant down regulated genes after SNC, we found the cytokines Ccl2, Il1b and Tnf, which we validated for their downregulation by qPCR experiments (Figure 3D and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNAseq data analysis, validated by qPCR, with supporting figure reference.

claim: Hematopoietic cell lineage pathway was down regulated specifically after DRC and SCI, but not after SNC.
source: Hematopoietic cell lineage pathway, which is involved in the formation of macrophages from myeloid cells, was down regulated specifically after DRC and SCI, but not after SNC (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the KEGG pathway analysis of the scRNAseq data, with supporting figure reference.

claim: The cell cycle and DNA replication pathways were upregulated only after SNC.
source: The cell cycle and DNA replication pathways were upregulated only after SNC (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the KEGG pathway analysis of the scRNAseq data, with supporting figure reference.

claim: Fenofibrate treatment improved axon regeneration after DRC.
source: We tested if fenofibrate treatment improved axon regeneration after DRC. Mice were fed with fenofibrate or control diet for 2 weeks as described (Avraham et al., 2020) and then underwent DRC injury. We measured the extent of axon regeneration past the injury site three days later by labeling dorsal root sections with SCG10, a marker for regenerating axons (Shin et al., 2014; Figure 7E). The crush site was determined according to highest SCG10 intensity along the nerve. First, we measured the length of the 10 longest axons, which reflect the extent of axon elongation, regardless of the number of axons that regenerate (Figure 7F). Second, we measured a regeneration index by normalizing the average SCG10 intensity at distances away from the crush site to the SCG10 intensity at the crush site (Figure 7G). This measure takes into accounts both the length and the number of regenerating axons past the crush site. Both measurement methods revealed improved regeneration in mice treated with fenofibrate compared to control diet (Figure 7F and G and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data presented in the study, with supporting figure references.
